Show model solution

Count overlaps first, then find which kernel words remain after excluding stabilizers. Each face has weight eight. Intersections of two, three, and four distinct faces have weights four, two, and one. A Z row is a face or pair intersection, so its overlap with an X face has weight eight, four, or two, always even. Unit-vector columns distinguish the four linear functions, proving X rank four.

Suppose a combination of the ten linear and quadratic Z-check functions vanishes on every nonzero label. Evaluating it on unit vectors forces the linear coefficients to vanish. Each weight-two vector then forces its quadratic coefficient to vanish. Thus the Z checks are independent:

rank⁡HX=4,rank⁡HZ=10,k=15−4−10=1.\operatorname{rank}H_X=4,\qquad \operatorname{rank}H_Z=10,\qquad k=15-4-10=1.rankHX​=4,rankHZ​=10,k=15−4−10=1.

The kernel ker⁡HX\ker H_XkerHX​ is the [15,11,3][15,11,3][15,11,3] Hamming code. Its distinct nonzero columns exclude kernel words of weight one or two. Any two columns sum to a third, giving a weight-three word. All Z stabilizers have even weight, so this word is logical and dZ=3d_Z=3dZ​=3.

The constant function and four linear functions satisfy HZH_ZHZ​ and are independent. They fill its five-dimensional kernel. Nonzero linear words have weight eight, their complements weight seven, and constant words weight zero or fifteen. The X stabilizers are the linear subspace. Removing them leaves dX=7d_X=7dX​=7 in the punctured Reed-Muller [15,5,7][15,5,7][15,5,7] kernel. Thus the sector distances are (7,3)(7,3)(7,3).

With three-bit labels, faces have weight four and pair overlaps two, giving Steane's Hamming rows. A pair-intersection Z row would overlap a third face once and anticommute. Omit those rows and use HZ=HXH_Z=H_XHZ​=HX​. Steane's coset weights zero/four and three/seven permit S-type phases.

For RM15, ∣0L⟩|0_L\rangle∣0L​⟩ has weights zero/eight and ∣1L⟩|1_L\rangle∣1L​⟩ weights seven/fifteen. Physical T=diag⁡(1,eiπ/4)T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})T=diag(1,eiπ/4) gives a word phase eiπw/4e^{i\pi w/4}eiπw/4. Every zero-coset term gets one; every one-coset term gets e−iπ/4e^{-i\pi/4}e−iπ/4. Therefore

T⊗15∣C=Tˉ†,(T†)⊗15∣C=Tˉ.T^{\otimes15}\big|_{\mathcal C}=\bar T^\dagger,\qquad (T^\dagger)^{\otimes15}\big|_{\mathcal C}=\bar T.T⊗15​C​=Tˉ†,(T†)⊗15​C​=Tˉ.

This is Eq. (5) in our phase convention A fault-tolerant one-way quantum computer, PDF pp. 3–4 Original source ↗ · DOI: 10.1016/j.aop.2006.01.012. Applying HHH to every physical qubit exchanges the X and Z row spaces. Their ranks are four and ten, so the exchanged spaces cannot equal the original ones. Thus H⊗15H^{\otimes15}H⊗15 is a transversal physical operation, but it does not preserve this code. Transversal T therefore exists on a code without a universal transversal gate set. Eastin-Knill forbids such a universal set for a code correcting arbitrary single-site errors Surviving as a Quantum Computer in a Classical World (draft textbook, 2026 draft), PDF p. 190, Theorem 11.7 Original source ↗. Module 9 develops this limit; Module 10 uses the code for distillation Surviving as a Quantum Computer in a Classical World (draft textbook, 2026 draft), PDF pp. 237–239; @raussendorf_2012_key_ideas, printed p. 4559, bibliographic reference Original source ↗.

Extra qubits help when recovery can remove local disturbances without learning or changing the stored information. Correcting an operator span lets a finite recovery handle coherent combinations from a continuum of possible errors.

For a fixed code, now assume independent stochastic data errors with probability ppp per qubit in the correction round. Suppose ideal recovery corrects every pattern through weight ttt. A logical failure then requires more than ttt faulty qubits. Such patterns have total probability O(pt+1)O(p^{t+1})O(pt+1) as ppp tends to zero, so the logical failure probability has the same upper-order scaling.

You can now use a check list to identify the code space, test recovery, and determine how Clifford gates and ancilla measurements act on the encoded information. Five data qubits achieve arbitrary single-qubit protection; no-cloning rules out four. In Module 3, the checks acquire a physical geometry.
